newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria hopes reforms will speed up EU admission.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria hopes reforms will speed up EU admission.

text.p: A limited deal reached at the European Union's Amsterdam summit boosts Bulgaria's hopes of meeting EU entry conditions once it has implemented economic reforms, officials said on Wednesday.

"The Amsterdam treaty shows a positive trend in seeking flexible enlargement formulas. A possible delay is not a bad sign, as it would give Bulgaria more time to prepare and meet admission conditions," Dimitar Ganchev, deputy head of the Foreign Ministry European Integration department, told Reuters.
The summit was supposed to resolve issues facing the 15 EU members so that they could begin accession talks with a first group of future entrants in six months' time.
But the updated treaty that was finally agreed left various questions undecided.

Bulgaria's economic crisis makes it one of the EU hopefuls with the least chance of joining in the first round. But the new government's commitment to a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime due for introduction on July 1 may boost its chances, economists said.

"The introduction of a currency board will contribute to the stabilisation of the economy and its gradual compliance with the Maastricht convergence criteria," Mariela Nenova, director of the government's Agency for Economic Analysis and Forecast (AEAF), told a seminar.
A currency board is a self-regulating monetary mechanism aimed at stabilising the local currency and curbing inflation.

"The currency board is a good basis for compliance with the convergence criteria. One of them, the stable foreign exchange rate, will be automatically fulfilled as long as the currency board functions," said AEAF's outgoing director Gancho Ganchev.
Under the system, the lev will be pegged to the mark as anchor currency at a rate of 1,000 levs per mark and levs in circulation must be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves.
Interest rates will also naturally converge to the level of interest rates of the anchor currency, the mark, plus a risk premium, said Ganchev.

Bulgaria's choice of the mark as an anchor currency links the economy to the advantages and disadvantages on the path to a single European currency on January 1, 1999, central bank board member Roumen Avramov told Reuters.
Other macro-economic targets will also be met in the course of a year if the currency board operates successfully, said Ganchev.

Joining the EU and NATO is a strategic priority of the new reformist government which took office last month but it has the difficult task of making up for seven years of delayed reforms, said Nenova.

Under agreements with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, Bulgaria must privatise as much as possible of its run-down economy this year to fund domestic and foreign debt payments, which comprise 9.8 percent of its gross domestic product.
The currency board system bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks.
Adapting the country's legislation, industry and farming to EU standards is part of the government's medium-term programme, said Nenova.
Bulgaria has an association accord with the European Union since 1993.
